What makes snails so fascinating?

Carrying its home on its back and crawling along slowly, the snail is a nature friend children meet on rainy days. There's plenty of science hidden in its slowness.

We've gathered all kinds of stories about snails, including their characteristics, their ecology, and observing pet snails.

content.alt: Snail - Nature and science facts about snails
content.text:
Nature and science facts about snails

Snails secrete sticky mucus so they can glide smoothly even over rough surfaces while keeping their bodies moist. Inside their mouth is a file-like radula for scraping and eating leaves. When threatened, they tuck themselves into their shell, and their eyes are at the tips of their tentacles. Many snails are hermaphrodites (both male and female in one body), and there are tens of thousands of species worldwide.

content.alt: Snail - Great things to observe together
content.text:
Great things to observe together

Point out things like the shell (a portable home and defense), the mucus (gliding and moisture), the tentacles (eyes), and the radula (scraping leaves). It's fun to talk together about "Why does a snail leave a sticky trail?" and "Where are its eyes?"

Parent guide: extending into observation and hands-on experience

After the rain, observe the shiny trail a snail leaves in the flower bed. Gently touch a tentacle to see it tuck in (softly), and watch it scrape a lettuce leaf to really understand the radula. (Return it to its place after observing.)

content.text:
Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)

Q. Where are a snail's eyes?
A. Its eyes are at the tips of its larger tentacles. It uses its tentacles to check its surroundings as it moves slowly.

Q. Why does a snail leave a sticky trail?
A. It secretes mucus so it can glide smoothly and keep its body moist.

Q. How can we observe them at home?
A. After the rain, use a magnifier to observe the mucus trail, tentacles, and leaf-scraping in the flower bed, then return it to its place.
